title: "The MGRS grid"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
```

`MGRSGrid` splits an area of interest (AOI) into the 10 km squares of the [Military Grid
Reference System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Grid_Reference_System) (MGRS). Each
square is an [`odc.geo`](https://odc-geo.readthedocs.io/) `GeoBox` with a fixed CRS, affine
transform and shape, so rasters resampled onto the same square at the same resolution line up
pixel for pixel.

A square's MGRS code and the resolution are enough to rebuild it. The grid is therefore a
specification, not a dataset: nothing has to be stored or shared to reproduce it.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "The twelve 10 km squares selected by an AOI in the Bernese Alps, each labelled with its MGRS code. The map is drawn in UTM zone 32N, where the squares are axis-aligned; the AOI (dashed) is a longitude–latitude box."
#| warning: false
import contextily as cx
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from shapely import box

from freezebase.mgrs import MGRSGrid

alps_box = box(7.8, 46.45, 8.15, 46.65)
alps = MGRSGrid(alps_box).to_geodataframe()
alps_utm = alps.to_crs(int(alps.epsg.iloc[0]))
alps_aoi = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[alps_box], crs=4326)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
alps_utm.plot(ax=ax, facecolor="tab:blue", alpha=0.15, edgecolor="tab:blue", linewidth=1.0)
for code, center in zip(alps_utm.mgrs_code, alps_utm.geometry.centroid):
    ax.annotate(code, (center.x, center.y), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9)
alps_aoi.to_crs(alps_utm.crs).boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--")
cx.add_basemap(ax, source=cx.providers.Esri.WorldGrayCanvas, crs=alps_utm.crs, attribution_size=6)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

## Why a fixed grid

Combining a Sentinel-1 scene, a Sentinel-2 composite, a DEM and a rasterised outline needs a
common grid, because each usually arrives in its own projection, resolution and tiling scheme.
`MGRSGrid` defines that grid independently of the inputs: for a given MGRS code and
resolution, every pipeline derives the same CRS, transform and shape. Sources resampled onto a
square are then pixel-aligned with each other.

## Why 10 km × 10 km MGRS squares

MGRS is an established metric reference system that Sentinel-2 already uses, and 10 km squares
are a practical size to process:

1. **Metric and established.** Each square lies on the metre-based lattice of a UTM zone and
   is axis-aligned in that projection, so a 10 m pixel is 10 m on the grid rather than a
   varying fraction of a degree.
2. **Shared with Sentinel-2.** A freezebase code such as `32TMS35` names a 10 km square inside
   the 100 km MGRS square of Sentinel-2 tile `T32TMS`. The parent tile is therefore visible in
   the code, and compatible 10 m data can be retiled without a grid shift.
3. **A practical unit of work.** At 10 m resolution, a 100 km square is 10,000 × 10,000 pixels
   and a 10 km square is 1,000 × 1,000. The smaller squares make it practical to download,
   cache and process only those touched by scattered AOIs.
4. **No overlap within a UTM zone.** Sentinel-2 product tiles are 109.8 km wide and overlap
   their neighbours[^1]. freezebase squares step by exactly 10 km, so squares of the same UTM
   zone never overlap. Squares of neighbouring zones can; see [Good to know](#good-to-know).

[^1]: Bauer-Marschallinger, B., & Falkner, K. (2023). Wasting petabytes: A
survey of the Sentinel-2 UTM tiling grid and its spatial overhead. *ISPRS
Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing*, 202, 682–690.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isprsjprs.2023.07.015>

## Select the squares for an AOI

`MGRSGrid` takes an AOI in WGS84 and selects every square that intersects it. This AOI around
Geneva crosses 6° E, the boundary between UTM zones 31 and 32:

```{python}
from shapely import box

from freezebase.mgrs import MGRSGrid

aoi = box(5.8, 46.0, 6.5, 46.4)  # bare Shapely means WGS84 here
grid = MGRSGrid(aoi)

len(grid)
```

`to_geodataframe()` returns one row per square, in WGS84:

```{python}
gdf = grid.to_geodataframe()
gdf.head()
```

Each row holds the square's MGRS code, its UTM zone and hemisphere, the native EPSG code and
the south-west corner in UTM metres. The EPSG column shows that this AOI spans two zones:

```{python}
gdf.groupby(["zone", "epsg"]).size()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## How squares are selected

- A bare Shapely geometry is taken to be in WGS84. A `GeoSeries` or `GeoDataFrame` must
  declare WGS84 explicitly.
- Every square that intersects the AOI is returned whole, so the grid covers slightly more
  than the AOI.
- A square that only touches the AOI boundary counts as intersecting.
- `resolution` sets the pixel size inside each square. It does not change which squares are
  selected.
:::

## Each square is a GeoBox

Indexing or iterating over the grid yields `MGRSGeoBox` objects, a subclass of
[`odc.geo.geobox.GeoBox`](https://odc-geo.readthedocs.io/en/latest/intro-geobox.html) that
adds the `mgrs_code`:

```{python}
square = grid[0]
square
```

A GeoBox is the CRS, affine transform and shape of a pixel grid:

```{python}
from odc.geo.geobox import GeoBox

print(f"mgrs_code:  {square.mgrs_code}")
print(f"crs:        {square.crs}")
print(f"shape:      {square.shape}")
print(f"resolution: {square.resolution}")
print(f"transform:\n{square.transform}")
print(f"is GeoBox:  {isinstance(square, GeoBox)}")
```

A square works wherever a GeoBox is accepted, and `odc.geo` properties such as `extent` and
`boundingbox` work on it. Operations that derive a different box, such as padding, slicing or
reprojection, return a plain `GeoBox` without `mgrs_code`, because the result no longer covers
the square the code names.

## Rebuild a square from its code

`MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs()` rebuilds a square from its code and resolution, so a code stored in
a filename, a database or a job description needs no AOI:

```{python}
from freezebase.mgrs import MGRSGeoBox, mgrs_to_crs

square = MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs("32TMS35", resolution=10.0)
print(square)
print(mgrs_to_crs(square.mgrs_code))
```

### Choosing a resolution

The resolution must be positive and divide 10 km evenly. Resolutions such as 10 m, 20 m and
100 m therefore give whole-pixel grids that nest into each other by an integer factor:

```{python}
for resolution in (10.0, 20.0, 100.0):
    cell = MGRSGeoBox.from_mgrs("32TMS35", resolution=resolution)
    print(f"{resolution:>5.0f} m -> {cell.shape}")
```

## Good to know {#good-to-know}

The grid covers 80° S to 84° N only. freezebase implements the UTM part of MGRS, not the polar
UPS grids.

Squares of neighbouring UTM zones can overlap. Each zone is projected on its own, and a square
along a zone edge is kept whole, so it can extend into the neighbouring zone. An AOI that
crosses the edge can therefore select squares from both zones that cover some of the same
ground. In exchange, every square stays square and axis-aligned in its own UTM CRS, and no
part of the AOI is left uncovered. Drawing the Geneva example in one map projection shows
the two grids:

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "The 10 km grids of UTM zones 31 and 32 over the Geneva AOI. Each is axis-aligned in its own projection, so they appear rotated and overlap near the boundary when displayed together."
#| warning: false
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
import pyproj

web_mercator = pyproj.CRS(3857)
squares = gdf.to_crs(web_mercator)
aoi_gdf = gpd.GeoDataFrame(geometry=[aoi], crs=4326).to_crs(web_mercator)
zone_colors = {31: "tab:blue", 32: "tab:red"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
for zone, color in zone_colors.items():
    squares[squares.zone == zone].plot(
        ax=ax, facecolor=color, alpha=0.25, edgecolor=color, linewidth=1.0
    )
aoi_gdf.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="black", linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--")
cx.add_basemap(ax, source=cx.providers.Esri.WorldGrayCanvas, crs=web_mercator, attribution_size=6)
ax.legend(
    handles=[
        *(
            Patch(facecolor=color, alpha=0.25, edgecolor=color, label=f"UTM zone {zone}")
            for zone, color in zone_colors.items()
        ),
        Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor="black", linestyle="--", label="AOI"),
    ],
    loc="lower right",
)
ax.set_axis_off()
```
